summary: V1 InputBatch.condense leaves a stale allowed_token_ids mask on recycled batch rows
description:
## Severity

- **Severity:** Low
- **CVSS v3.1:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N` (3.7, Low)
- **CWE:** CWE-440 (Expected Behavior Violation), CWE-668 (Exposure of Resource to Wrong Sphere)

## Summary

vLLM V1 `InputBatch.condense()` can leave a stale `allowed_token_ids_mask_cpu_tensor` row after moving a constrained request. A later unrestricted request that reuses that batch slot inherits the previous request's token allowlist, so sampling for that other client is constrained by a mask it did not set (cross-request output-integrity issue). The victim request still returns HTTP 200 with no error indication.

Public report: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/43894

## Affected

- **Ecosystem / package:** pip / `vllm`
- **Affected versions:** vLLM ≤ 0.30.0 (V1 worker `InputBatch` path). Confirmed via public issue #43894.
- **Fixed versions:** Fix merged in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/43931 (not yet in a tagged release as of v0.30.0; expected in the next release).

## Details

`InputBatch.condense()` copies `allowed_token_ids_mask_cpu_tensor` from a moved request's row into the freed index but never clears the source row. `add_request()` only writes that row when the new request sets `sampling_params.allowed_token_ids`. When another active request still has `allowed_token_ids`, `_make_sampling_metadata()` copies the active prefix of the CPU mask to GPU and `Sampler.apply_logits_processors()` applies the stale whitelist to the unrestricted request.

An attacker who can submit generate traffic (including unauthenticated `/invocations`, which is outside `--api-key` guards, or any valid API key on `/v1`) plants a chosen `allowed_token_ids` mask. If batching/`condense` recycles that row onto another client's unrestricted request while the constrained request is still active, the victim's tokens are limited to the attacker's allowlist (for example only a single token, only digit tokens, or only tokens that spell a short phrase). This is vocabulary steering / wrong allowlist application, not free-form substitution of arbitrary attacker text.

A related but distinct bug in `InputBatch.swap_states()` (row-view aliasing of the same mask tensor) was fixed in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48419.

## Impact

Limited cross-request sampling integrity on a shared engine: one client's `allowed_token_ids` can constrain another client's outputs under concurrent batching. Confidentiality and availability are unaffected. Attack complexity is High because exploitation needs concurrent requests plus a `condense` slot-reuse race while the attacker's constrained request remains in the batch.

## Patches

- https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/43931 — clear vacated `allowed_token_ids` mask rows in `condense()`
- https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48419 — related `swap_states` mask aliasing fix

## References

- https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/43894
- https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/43931
- https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48419
- https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/usage/security.html (API key does not cover `/invocations`)

## Credit

Reported publicly by @glaziermag in issue #43894.

cwes.name: Exposure of Resource to Wrong Sphere

summary: Forged multimodal UUID + P0/P1 processor-cache eviction drift: unauthenticated remote crash of the whole vLLM engine
description:
## Summary

Multimodal content parts (`image_url`, `video_url`, `input_audio`, ...) accept a user-supplied `uuid` field that vLLM uses **verbatim as the item's cache identity** (`mm_hash`). The two frontend/engine processor caches (P0 "sender" cache in the API process, P1 "receiver" cache in the EngineCore process) are independent LRU caches whose evictions are **not synchronized**, and the P1 hit path performs **zero consistency validation** — it silently substitutes the cached item's tensor data for whatever the current request actually contains.

A single unauthenticated client can exploit this to kill the entire engine, deterministically, with default server flags:

1. **Seed**: send a small image with `uuid="U"`. Both caches now map `U` to an item with **N_A** visual tokens (e.g. 4).
2. **Drift**: send ~70 requests, each carrying a *unique* uuid, a max-size image, and an over-long text prompt. Each request is rejected with 400 — but **after** its image has been inserted into the P0 cache (insertion happens during chat rendering, before prompt-length validation), so these requests fill P0 **without ever reaching the engine/P1**. `U` is evicted from P0 only.
3. **Kill**: send a *large* image with `uuid="U"`. P0 misses → the image is freshly processed and the prompt is spliced with **N_B** (e.g. 2048+) placeholder tokens; the request carries full data to the engine, but P1 still has `U` → the engine **discards the fresh data and substitutes the stale N_A-row tensor**. The scheduler plans for N_B encoder slots while the worker merges N_A embeddings into N_B placeholders → `ValueError: Attempted to assign 4 = 4 multimodal tokens to 2048 placeholders` at `vllm/model_executor/models/utils.py:711` → uncaught in the EngineCore busy loop → `_send_engine_dead()` → the EngineCore process dies, every API server reports `EngineDeadError` and shuts down. `/health` never recovers; the deployment needs a full restart.

Verified end-to-end on the official `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.29.0` image with Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct, default configuration (no flags beyond `--served-model-name`/`--gpu-memory-utilization`): after 70 flood requests the kill request returned `500 EngineCore encountered an issue` and `/health` went dead permanently. The vulnerable code is byte-identical on `main` (post-0.29.0).

## Details

**1. The client-controlled `uuid` becomes the cache hash verbatim.** `vllm/entrypoints/chat_utils.py:1677` / `:1884-1886` read `part["uuid"]` per content part and pass it through as `mm_uuids`. In `vllm/multimodal/processing/inputs.py:62-63`, when no `hf_processor_mm_kwargs` are present (the default for chat requests), the uuid string **is** the item hash — no content binding at all:

```python
# vllm/multimodal/processing/inputs.py:62-63
else:
    hashes.append(uuid_item)        # client string used verbatim as mm_hash
```

**2. P0 insertion happens before request validation.** In the serving path, `render_chat_request` (`vllm/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/serving.py:275`) runs full mm processing — `mm_processor.apply` (`vllm/renderers/base.py:759`) → `_cached_apply_hf_processor` → `_merge_mm_kwargs` → `cache.get_and_update_item` (`vllm/multimodal/processing/processor.py:1338`), which inserts the processed item into the P0 sender cache (default `mm_processor_cache_type="lru"`, 4 GiB). Only afterwards does `get_max_tokens` (`vllm/entrypoints/serve/utils/api_utils.py:183-186`) reject over-long prompts with 400. **A request can therefore write to P0 while never reaching the engine** — the primitive that desynchronizes P0 from P1. (Public issue #43941 documented this same asymmetry for the opposite drift direction, which was later handled via `MultiModalCacheMissError`; the P0-miss/P1-hit direction below was never addressed.)

**3. P1 substitutes cached data on hash hit with no consistency check.** In the EngineCore input thread, `preprocess_add_request` (`vllm/v1/engine/core.py:997-1000`) calls `mm_receiver_cache.get_and_update_features`, which only replaces `feature.data` (`vllm/multimodal/cache.py:673-690`) and keeps the request's own `mm_position` (placeholder layout). On a cache hit the receiver cache returns the stale item wholesale:

```python
# vllm/multimodal/cache.py:739-740  (MultiModalReceiverCache.get_and_update_item)
if (cached_item := self._cache.get(mm_hash)) is not None:
    return cached_item              # fresh data silently discarded; no size/modality check
```

Only the opposite drift (P0 hit / P1 miss, `data=None`) is handled, via the retryable `MultiModalCacheMissError`. Nothing validates that the cached item's modality, shape, or token count matches the current request's placeholders.

**4. The mismatch is fatal to the engine.** The scheduler plans encoder work from the request's (fresh) placeholder count N_B, while the worker gathers embeddings from the stale N_A-row tensor (encoder-cache hit under the same forged hash, or re-encoding the stale data — both yield N_A rows). `_merge_multimodal_embeddings` then raises:

```python
# vllm/model_executor/models/utils.py:703-714
inputs_embeds[is_multimodal] = mm_embeds_flat.to(dtype=input_dtype)   # RuntimeError
...
raise ValueError(
    f"Attempted to assign {expr} = {num_actual_tokens} "
    f"multimodal tokens to {num_expected_tokens} placeholders") from e
```

This exception is raised inside the worker's input preparation with no per-request containment, propagates to the EngineCore busy loop's top-level handler (`vllm/v1/engine/core.py:1372`), and triggers `_send_engine_dead()`. The API server's `output_handler` receives `EngineDeadError` (`vllm/v1/engine/async_llm.py:819`) and the whole process tree shuts down. (Issue #55546 independently reported this sink — "one bad multimodal item kills the entire V1 engine tree" — from an organically occurring stale cache entry; this report provides the missing deterministic, remote, single-attacker trigger.)

**Cost of the attack.** With the default `mm_processor_cache_gb=4`, one max-size Qwen2.5-VL image (12845056 pixels) caches as ~77 MB, so ~56 flood requests suffice; we used 70. Flood requests are CPU-only image decodes (~0.3 s each here) and can be issued sequentially or concurrently; the total wall-clock cost of the kill was under one minute. Models with larger `max_pixels` fill the cache in even fewer requests. Note that issuing the flood with *successful* requests does not work — they would populate P1 as well; rejection after P0 insertion is essential, and the over-long-prompt 400 is one always-available way to get it (no size limits depend on non-default flags).


## Impact

Any unauthenticated client that can reach a multimodal vLLM endpoint (`/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/responses`, etc. — all accept content-part `uuid`) can **deterministically crash the entire serving instance**: the EngineCore process dies, every in-flight request fails, and the API server exits; the deployment stays down until restarted. In data-parallel or multi-API-server deployments the blast radius extends to the whole engine group (cf. the DP8 outage in #55546). The attack requires no special privileges, no non-default server flags, no race conditions, and costs under a minute of sequential requests at default cache sizes.

This is distinct from the documented "Multimodal Media UUID Security" guidance in `docs/usage/security.md`, which covers only **integrity/confidentiality** consequences of uuid collisions (a caller silently receiving another caller's media). The guidance does not mention availability, and following it does not help: the attacker here deliberately collides with *their own* uuid, and the fatal element is the missing consistency check on the P1 hit path plus the unsynchronized eviction of the two caches.

**Suggested remediation** (any one of these breaks the kill chain):

1. On a P1 receiver-cache hit, validate the cached item against the request's `mm_position` (modality and expected embedding count); on mismatch, treat it as a miss (`MultiModalCacheMissError`) or reject the request — never substitute silently.
2. Make the feature/placeholder count mismatch in `_merge_multimodal_embeddings` a per-request error instead of a fatal engine exception (also requested by #55546).
3. Bind server-side cache identity to content even when a uuid is provided (e.g. `hash(content) + uuid`), eliminating forged-hash cache hits entirely.
4. Synchronize P0/P1 evictions (the engine already pushes `invalidate` to P0 on cache-miss; eviction-direction sync would close the remaining drift).

A public fix is available here: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57833

summary: An oversized min_tokens in one request hangs the vLLM engine while /health stays green
description:
## Summary

Any client that can reach `/inference/v1/generate`, mounted by default in v0.29.0 and unauthenticated unless `--api-key` is set, can stop `vllm serve` from serving with one request. The body sets `sampling_params.max_tokens` to `null` and `min_tokens` to 2147483648. The EngineCore, the single scheduler process, re-validates it in its input thread, which dies; the process stays up, `/health` answers 200, every later request hangs.

## Root cause

The `min_tokens <= max_tokens` check runs in [`_verify_args`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/c1b69aa0d49b88016b5b2156ae61649c2c2df282/vllm/sampling_params.py#L616-L620) only when `max_tokens` is set. On `/inference/v1/generate` the API process builds `SamplingParams` [directly from the JSON](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/c1b69aa0d49b88016b5b2156ae61649c2c2df282/vllm/entrypoints/scale_out/token_in_token_out/protocol.py#L209) with `max_tokens=None`, so the check is skipped; the processor then [fills in `max_tokens`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/c1b69aa0d49b88016b5b2156ae61649c2c2df282/vllm/v1/engine/input_processor.py#L358-L362) (2045 here) without validating again and forwards the request.

In the EngineCore, [`process_input_sockets`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/c1b69aa0d49b88016b5b2156ae61649c2c2df282/vllm/v1/engine/core.py#L1757) decodes the message, which rebuilds `SamplingParams` and runs `_verify_args` a second time. Now both values are present and `VLLMValidationError` is raised on the decode line, one line above the `try` that protects request handling:

```python
1757                        req: EngineCoreRequest = add_request_decoder.decode(data_frames)  # <-
1758                        try:
1759                            request = self.preprocess_add_request(req)
...
1765                        except Exception:
1766                            self._handle_request_preproc_error(req)
1767                            continue
```

The exception is not caught, so the thread exits. It was the only reader of the input socket: no request reaches the scheduler any more, but nothing reports it, because the scheduler loop just waits on an empty queue, the thread is checked [only at start-up](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/c1b69aa0d49b88016b5b2156ae61649c2c2df282/vllm/v1/engine/core.py#L1135-L1136), and [`check_health`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/c1b69aa0d49b88016b5b2156ae61649c2c2df282/vllm/v1/engine/async_llm.py#L1025-L1028) only looks for a recorded error. `/health` keeps answering 200 while every generation request hangs.

The OpenAI routes resolve `max_tokens` before building `SamplingParams`, so there the check runs in the API process and returns HTTP 400.


## Impact

- **Who can trigger it** — Any network client, no credentials, that can reach `/inference/v1/generate`: mounted by default on a `vllm serve` of v0.29.0, and on main when `VLLM_ENABLE_SCALE_OUT_ENDPOINTS=1` or `--tokens-only` is set.
- **What they get** — One 92-byte request stops the server from serving any route for every client; later requests hang until the client gives up. The process stays alive and `/health` keeps answering 200, so nothing restarts it. Recovery is a manual restart.

---
The initial discovery was made by AI scanning tools in Microsoft Security FORGE Labs, and later all technical claims has been reviewed and validated by human experts.

A public fix is available here: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57731

cwes.name: Improper Check for Unusual or Exceptional Conditions

summary: Qwen2-VL / Qwen3-VL video samplers bound on request-controlled max_frames, which the num_frames ceiling does not reach
description:
### Summary

An unauthenticated remote attacker can exhaust the memory of the vLLM API-server process by raising the request-level `media_io_kwargs.video.max_frames` and `fps` knobs on any deployment serving a Qwen2-VL or Qwen3-VL model. 74 extra bytes of JSON took the server's peak RSS from 2 271 MiB to 13 629 MiB over unauthenticated `POST /tokenize`.

The `num_frames` ceiling reported in GHSA-vxqj-p4gw-9h4c and fixed by open PR #51969 does not reach this path: the Qwen samplers do not read `num_frames` at all. The same knobs were already capped upstream for `GLMGAVideoBackend` as an accepted security fix in `8b6de0eb9` (PR #54935, merged 2026-09-04); that cap never reached Qwen.

### Details

#### Relationship to GHSA-vxqj-p4gw-9h4c and PR #51969 (read this first)

GHSA-vxqj-p4gw-9h4c reported that request-level `media_io_kwargs.video.num_frames` overrides the engine frame-count ceiling, and open PR #51969 fixes it by clamping `num_frames` inside `VideoMediaIO.merge_kwargs`.

That clamp does not reach the Qwen samplers. `Qwen2VLVideoBackend` and `Qwen3VLVideoBackend` do not read `num_frames` at all — `Qwen2VLVideoBackend`'s own docstring says so ("``num_frames`` is ignored (fps-driven, like the Qwen3-VL loader)"). They bound on `max_frames`, read from the same merged dict with no ceiling:

```python
# vllm/multimodal/video.py — Qwen3VLVideoBackend.compute_frames_index_to_sample
min_frames = kwargs.get("min_frames", 4)
max_frames = kwargs.get("max_frames", 768)
num_frames = int(total_frames_num / original_fps * fps)
num_frames = min(max(num_frames, min_frames), max_frames, total_frames_num)
```

With `max_frames` raised from the request, the only remaining bound is `total_frames_num` — every frame in the container.

I applied PR #51969's patch locally and re-ran both paths through the real merge layer (`merge_media_io_kwargs` → `VideoMediaIO.merge_kwargs` → `MediaConnector`), against `main` @ `b23433088`:

| request `media_io_kwargs.video` | merged kwargs after #51969 | frames decoded | peak RSS |
|---|---|---|---|
| *(absent)* | `None` | 32 | 706 MiB |
| `{"video_backend":"opencv","num_frames":-1}` | `{…,"num_frames":32}` | **32 — fixed** | 706 MiB |
| `{"video_backend":"qwen3_vl"}` | `{…,"num_frames":32}` | 60 | 779 MiB |
| `{"video_backend":"qwen3_vl","max_frames":1e9,"fps":1e6}` | `{…,"max_frames":1000000000,"fps":1000000,"num_frames":32}` | **900 — survives** | **2 994 MiB** |

#51969 does exactly what it claims for `num_frames`; the clamp writes `num_frames: 32` into the merged dict and the Qwen sampler ignores it, while `max_frames` and `fps` pass through untouched.

#### The codebase already has the fix pattern, on other backends

This is not a new control being proposed. Commit `8b6de0eb9` — "[Security] Cap GLMGA video sampling to prevent request-driven resource exhaustion" (PR #54935, merged 2026-09-04, same author as #51969) — caps precisely these two knobs for `GLMGAVideoBackend`:

```python
_MAX_FRAMES: ClassVar[int] = 640
_MAX_FPS: ClassVar[int] = 30
...
target_fps = min(target.fps, cls._MAX_FPS)
max_frames = min(kwargs.get("max_frames", cls._MAX_FRAMES), cls._MAX_FRAMES)
```

Its description states the root cause as "both `target_fps` and `max_frames` are controllable via request-level `media_io_kwargs`", and says it follows "the pattern established by `GLM46VVideoBackend`" (which caps via `_MAX_FRAME_COUNT_DYNAMIC = 640` and `_MAX_DURATION = 2400`).

So two backends cap request-controlled `fps`/`max_frames` as an accepted security measure. `Qwen2VLVideoBackend` and `Qwen3VLVideoBackend` — the most widely deployed video models on vLLM — cap neither. In GLMGA the uncapped knobs sized an intermediate *index list*; in the Qwen samplers they size the *decoded frame buffer*, which is larger by the per-frame pixel count.

#### Reachability — default configuration, no authentication

* `media_io_kwargs` is a request body field on `ChatCompletionRequest` and is carried by `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/embeddings`, `/v1/responses`, `/tokenize` and `/invocations`. No flag gates it.
* `api_key` defaults to `None` (`vllm/entrypoints/launchers/cli_args.py`), and `AuthenticationMiddleware` is installed only when a key is configured — a default `vllm serve` is entirely unauthenticated.
* Even with `--api-key` set, `GUARDED_PREFIX = ("/v1", "/v2", "/inference", "/cohere")` (`vllm/entrypoints/serve/middleware/authenticate.py:11`), so `/invocations` — which validates the same `ChatCompletionRequest` body — and `/tokenize` — which performs full media ingestion — remain unauthenticated.
* `MediaConnector.fetch_video` applies the model's registered sampler only when the request did not name one (`if "video_backend" not in video_io_kwargs`), so `video_backend: "qwen3_vl"` is selectable on any deployment; request-level selection of stock sampler subclasses is already established as reachable by GHSA-j682-9xp5-rrf3. On a Qwen deployment no `video_backend` key is needed at all.
* Default-on for any video-capable Qwen model.

**The Rust frontend is not affected.** `rust/src/server/src/routes/openai/chat_completions/validate.rs:90` rejects `media_io_kwargs` with "media_io_kwargs is not supported." No second front is needed.

### Impact

Unauthenticated remote denial of service by memory exhaustion of the API-server process. The decode runs in the frontend during chat parsing, before scheduling or admission control, so every tenant on the instance is affected. `--limit-mm-per-prompt` does not apply — it bounds media *items*, not frames within an item. CWE-770 / CWE-400.

Measured over unauthenticated HTTP: 1.43 MiB request body, 74 extra bytes of JSON, server peak RSS 2 271 → 13 629 MiB. In-process, the same request takes the decode from 60 to 900 frames. The frame count is bounded only by `total_frames_num`, which is the attacker's choice of video, and decoded bytes are `frames × H × W × 3`.

**Context, measured on the `num_frames` path (GHSA-vxqj-p4gw-9h4c's path), not this one** — these figures show what an unbounded frame count costs once the source video is chosen for it, and they transfer to this path because both converge on the same `_read_frames_no_recovery` allocation:

* 5.74 MiB request body → 9.27 GiB decoded, 9.73 GiB of new resident memory (1 736×).
* 117.6 MiB `video/jpeg` payload → process OOM-killed: `Out of memory: Killed process 182667 (python) total-vm:38665704kB, anon-rss:21121616kB`

I did not re-run those two at the larger sizes through the Qwen sampler; the 900-frame figure above is what I measured on this path.

**Proposed CVSS v3.1:** `AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H` (7.5, High). Comparable advisories in this subsystem were published as Moderate; maintainers may prefer that for consistency.

### Suggested fix

Extend the ceiling to the sampler-side knobs rather than clamping the single `num_frames` key. Two options, either acceptable:

1. **Per-backend caps, matching `8b6de0eb9`.** Give `Qwen2VLVideoBackend` and `Qwen3VLVideoBackend` the `_MAX_FRAMES` / `_MAX_FPS` treatment already applied to `GLMGAVideoBackend`, so `kwargs.get("max_frames", …)` and `target.fps` are clamped to class constants. Smallest change; consistent with the accepted precedent. It leaves `Glm5NextVideoBackend`, `Molmo2VideoBackend`, `NemotronVLVideoBackend`, `DynamicVideoBackend` and `OpenCVDynamicOpenPanguVideoBackend` to be audited one by one, which is the current trajectory (#55727, #56207, #56390).
2. **Strip the frame-count knobs at the merge boundary.** In `VideoMediaIO.merge_kwargs`, drop `max_frames` / `min_frames` / `fps` from `runtime_kwargs` the way `hw_decoders`, `pool_size`, `device` and unconfigured GPU backends are already dropped there. That treats the whole frame-count family as startup-only in one place and is robust to future sampler subclasses, at the cost of removing a request-level knob some users may rely on. A clamp-don't-strip variant (request may lower, never raise) preserves the feature.

Option 2 composes with #51969 and needs no per-backend audit; I would favour it, but option 1 is the more conservative change and matches what has already been merged.

### Affected versions

`>= 0.24.0`, through v0.29.1rc0 and `main` @ `b23433088`.

Lower bound established by probing release tags through the GitHub contents API; no version below is inferred, each was read out of the file at that tag.

**Confirmed present — Qwen samplers reading unclamped `max_frames`** (`max_frames = kwargs.get("max_frames", 768)` inside `Qwen2VLVideoBackend` / `Qwen3VLVideoBackend` in `vllm/multimodal/video.py`):

| ref | `Qwen3VLVideoBackend` present | unclamped `max_frames` |
|---|---|---|
| v0.23.0 | no (class does not exist) | n/a |
| v0.24.0 | yes | yes |
| v0.25.0, v0.26.0, v0.27.0, v0.28.0, v0.29.0, v0.29.1rc0 | yes | yes |
| `main` @ `b23433088` | yes | yes |

**Confirmed present — request-level `media_io_kwargs`** (field on the chat request model, and `VideoMediaIO.merge_kwargs` present): every ref probed, v0.19.0 through v0.29.1rc0 and `main` @ `b23433088`.

**Confirmed absent — any `num_frames` ceiling clamp** (PR #51969 unmerged): every ref probed, v0.19.0 through v0.29.1rc0 and `main` @ `b23433088`.

**Not resolved, and why:**

1. The introducing commit/PR for `Qwen2VLVideoBackend` / `Qwen3VLVideoBackend`. My clone is shallow (`--depth=300`), so `git log -S'max_frames'` cannot reach it; the v0.23.0 → v0.24.0 boundary above is the tightest bound I established by probing release tags.
2. The rc tags between v0.23.0 and v0.24.0, to tighten the lower bound to a specific release candidate.
3. Whether a `max_frames` knob on a *differently named* pre-v0.24.0 backend is separately affected — at v0.23.0 `GLMGAVideoBackend` already carried `max_frames = kwargs.get("max_frames", 640)` with no clamp, and that clamp was only added on 2026-09-04 by `8b6de0eb9`. Versions between are plausibly affected through GLMGA rather than Qwen; I did not test that path.
4. Whether GHSA-vxqj-p4gw-9h4c's own affected range differs, which I cannot see — the advisory returns 404 to me.

No dependency versions are asserted anywhere in this report.

### Weaknesses of this report, stated upfront

* **No GPU was used.** This host has no CUDA device, so the HTTP results come from the in-tree GPU-less render server rather than a full `vllm serve`. That server runs the real frontend — the same request model, the same `merge_media_io_kwargs` → `VideoMediaIO.merge_kwargs` → `MediaConnector.fetch_video` chain, the same `/tokenize` route — and media decoding happens entirely in the frontend, so I do not believe the engine's presence changes the result. I have not confirmed that on a GPU deployment, and a reviewer may reasonably want that repeated under `vllm serve`.
* The in-process measurements (the #51969 comparison table) were taken by importing the tree directly at `b23433088`, verified by `__file__`, with no `vllm` wheel installed.
* **Amplification figures are a floor.** The OpenCV build available here offers only `mp4v`/`XVID`, giving ~2 200× compression on static content. An attacker using x264/x265 would do materially better for the same frame count.
* The two large figures in the Impact section (9.73 GiB RSS; the OOM kill) were measured on the `num_frames` path, not this one, and are labelled as such.
* Per-frame pixels remain bounded by `VLLM_MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`; this concerns the unbounded frame *count*, which multiplies it.
* `VLLM_MAX_MEDIA_DOWNLOAD_SIZE_MB` (default 256) caps the compressed size of an HTTP-fetched video but not a `data:` URI, which `MediaConnector.load_from_url` dispatches before any size logic is reached.

### If this is already covered

If GHSA-vxqj-p4gw-9h4c already covers the sampler-side knobs (`max_frames`, `min_frames`, `fps`) and not only `num_frames`, please close this as a duplicate — it is filed privately rather than raised on PR #51969 precisely to avoid describing an unfixed path in the open.

---

*Prepared with AI assistance (Claude), per the repository's contributing guidance on disclosing AI-assisted contributions. All findings were verified by executing vLLM's own code at the commits cited; the analysis and the claims are my own.*

*Reported by Eva Crystal / 0xiviel (XSource Security).*

summary: MOSS-Audio request-controlled processor cache permits remote memory exhaustion
description:
### Summary

  When vLLM serves a MOSS-Audio model, a client that can access the /tokenize endpoint can provide request-controlled
  mm_processor_kwargs.

  MOSS-Audio uses these values to construct MossAudioProcessor instances and stores every distinct instance in an
  unbounded private dictionary. Each processor contains a WhisperFeatureExtractor with an allocated mel-filter array.

  An attacker can therefore:

  1. Repeatedly submit distinct processor configurations to cause persistent linear memory growth.
  2. Supply oversized mel_config values to amplify the allocation made by a single request.

  This can exhaust host memory and terminate or severely degrade the API process. /tokenize is intentionally outside
  vLLM’s API-key-protected route prefixes, so --api-key alone does not restrict access to this endpoint.

  ### Details

  TokenizeChatRequest accepts arbitrary mm_processor_kwargs
  (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/bf7eee9d7b2788bafe69f0c21fde6af22a2d3319/vllm/entrypoints/serve/tokenize/protocol.py#L107-L110).

  The request reaches multimodal processing through:

  1. ServingTokenization.create_tokenize()

     (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/bf7eee9d7b2788bafe69f0c21fde6af22a2d3319/vllm/entrypoints/serve/tokenize/serving.py#L84-L92)

  2. OnlineRenderer.preprocess_chat()

     (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/bf7eee9d7b2788bafe69f0c21fde6af22a2d3319/vllm/renderers/online_renderer.py#L675-L704)

  3. BaseRenderer._process_multimodal()

     (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/bf7eee9d7b2788bafe69f0c21fde6af22a2d3319/vllm/renderers/base.py#L846-L880)

  4. MossAudioMultiModalProcessor._apply_hf_processor_main()

     (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/bf7eee9d7b2788bafe69f0c21fde6af22a2d3319/vllm/model_executor/models/moss_audio.py#L1358-L1400)

  Although /tokenize sets skip_mm_cache=True, this only selects the read-only multimodal processor. Its
  MossAudioProcessingInfo object still maintains the vulnerable private cache.

  The following request-controlled fields are used as cache-key components:

  - audio_token_id
  - audio_start_id
  - audio_end_id
  - enable_time_marker
  - mel_config

  MossAudioProcessingInfo.get_hf_processor()
  (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/bf7eee9d7b2788bafe69f0c21fde6af22a2d3319/vllm/model_executor/models/moss_audio.py#L1248-L1304)
  creates _hf_processor_cache as a plain dictionary. It has no capacity limit, TTL, or eviction policy.

  For every new key, it constructs a MossAudioProcessor
  (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/bf7eee9d7b2788bafe69f0c21fde6af22a2d3319/vllm/model_executor/models/moss_audio.py#L962-L997),
  which creates a WhisperFeatureExtractor.

  The default mel-filter array has:

  shape: (201, 128)
  dtype: float64
  size: 205,824 bytes

  Consequently, each unique default configuration retains approximately 206 KB in the mel-filter array alone.

  Request-controlled mel_config can amplify this substantially. The bounded configuration:

  {
    "mel_dim": 512,
    "mel_n_fft": 1024
  }

  creates:

  shape: (513, 512)
  dtype: float64
  size: 2,101,248 bytes

  The approximate final mel-filter allocation is:

  (floor(mel_n_fft / 2) + 1) * mel_dim * 8 bytes

  There are no effective upper bounds on these values. For example, mel_dim=65536 and mel_n_fft=65536 would attempt to
  allocate approximately 16 GiB for the final mel-filter array alone. This destructive value was not executed.

  Clearing the normal multimodal processor cache does not clear _hf_processor_cache, so these processors remain
  reachable for the lifetime of the frontend process.

  The project’s security documentation
  (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/bf7eee9d7b2788bafe69f0c21fde6af22a2d3319/docs/usage/security.md#L185-L214)
  documents /tokenize as an endpoint that does not require an API key.

  Suggested remediation is to reject request-level overrides of processor-construction parameters, validate strict upper
  bounds for mel dimensions, and either eliminate this dynamic cache or replace it with a small bounded cache that is
  also cleared by cache-reset operations.

 

  ### Impact

  An attacker who can reach a vLLM HTTP server serving a MOSS-Audio model can cause persistent attacker-controlled
  memory allocations in the frontend API process.

  Repeated unique configurations cause linear retained-memory growth. Oversized mel_config values can also cause a very
  large allocation from a single request. Continued exploitation can terminate the process through out-of-memory
  exhaustion, resulting in denial of service.

  The issue is limited to deployments serving a MOSS-Audio model. A reverse proxy that authenticates or rate-limits /
  tokenize can reduce exposure, but vLLM’s own --api-key setting does not protect this endpoint.

summary: Unbounded Prometheus label cardinality from attacker-controlled HTTP method tokens in the vLLM Rust frontend metrics middleware (unauthenticated denial of service)
description: [attachment.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/31987183/attachment.zip) ### Summary The Rust frontend of vLLM (`vllm-rs`, enabled via `VLLM_USE_RUST_FRONTEND=1` or by running the `vllm-rs` binary directly) records Prometheus HTTP metrics in the middleware `track_http_metrics`. It uses the **raw HTTP method token** of each request (`req.method().as_str()`) as a Prometheus label value, with no method allowlist, no label normalization, and no cardinality cap. An unauthenticated remote attacker can send requests with unique, arbitrary method tokens (e.g. `XVULNCARD000001 /tokenize HTTP/1.1`) to any registered route; the request is answered with 405 by axum's method router but still flows through the metrics middleware, permanently inserting new label sets into the global `http_requests` counter family and `http_request_duration_seconds` histogram family. Memory grows unboundedly until the process is OOM-killed, and every `/metrics` scrape becomes larger and more expensive to render. ### Details - `hyper`/`httparse` accept arbitrary tokens as HTTP methods, and axum's `MethodRouter` answers wrong-method requests on a registered path with 405 **from inside the route service**, which is wrapped by `Router::layer(from_fn(track_http_metrics))` (`src/rust/src/server/src/routes.rs:174`). The middleware therefore runs for these 405 responses and records `method = `, `handler = `, `status = "4xx"`. - `Family::get_or_create` in the `prometheus_client` crate inserts a **permanent** HashMap entry keyed by the label set. There is no TTL, no cap, and no eviction: each unique method token pins roughly `O(token length)` bytes in two label sets plus counter/histogram structures for the lifetime of the process. - The API-key middleware only guards the `/v1`, `/v2` and `/inference` path prefixes (`src/rust/src/server/src/middleware/auth.rs:16`). `/tokenize` and `/detokenize` are not guarded **and** are not in the metrics `EXCLUDED_HANDLERS` list, so the attack works **even when `--api-key` is configured**: an unauthenticated attacker can inject unbounded label cardinality through `/tokenize` 405s. Without `--api-key` (the default), every registered route works. - `/metrics` itself is unauthenticated and renders the entire registry into a single `String` on every scrape (`Metrics::render`, `src/rust/src/metrics/src/lib.rs:62-66`). With ~10^6 injected series, each scrape materializes hundreds of megabytes of text, amplifying CPU/memory pressure onto the server and the Prometheus monitoring stack (cardinality bomb). - Damage is **cumulative and permanent**: unlike request-flooding, the leaked memory is not reclaimed when the attack stops, and rate limiting does not help because each method token only needs to be seen once. ### Vulnerable code `src/rust/src/server/src/middleware/metrics.rs` (lines 34-71): ```rust pub async fn track_http_metrics(req: Request, next: Next) -> Response { let method = req.method().as_str().to_string(); // raw method token, no allowlist/normalization let handler = req .extensions() .get::() .map_or_else(|| "none".to_string(), |path| path.as_str().to_string()); let excluded = EXCLUDED_HANDLERS.contains(&handler.as_str()); let started_at = Instant::now(); let response = next.run(req).await; if excluded { return response; } let elapsed = started_at.elapsed().as_secs_f64(); let status = status_group(response.status().as_u16()); let metrics = &METRICS.api_server; metrics .http_requests .get_or_create(&HttpRequestLabels { method: method.clone(), // permanently inserts a new series per unique token status, handler: handler.clone(), }) .inc(); metrics .http_request_duration_seconds .get_or_create(&HttpHandlerLabels { method, handler }) .observe(elapsed); metrics.http_request_duration_highr_seconds.observe(elapsed); response } ``` `src/rust/src/metrics/src/api_server.rs` (lines 26-41) - label sets keyed by the raw method string: ```rust #[derive(Clone, Debug, Hash, PartialEq, Eq, EncodeLabelSet)] pub struct HttpRequestLabels { pub method: String, pub status: &'static str, pub handler: String, } #[derive(Clone, Debug, Hash, PartialEq, Eq, EncodeLabelSet)] pub struct HttpHandlerLabels { pub method: String, pub handler: String, } pub(crate) type HttpRequestCounterFamily = Family; pub(crate) type HttpHandlerHistogramFamily = Family Histogram>; ``` `src/rust/src/server/src/middleware/auth.rs` (line 16) - `/tokenize` is not guarded, so the attack bypasses `--api-key`: ```rust const GUARDED_PREFIXES: &[&str] = &["/v1", "/v2", "/inference"]; ``` ### PoC ```http XVULNCARD000001 /tokenize HTTP/1.1 Host: TARGET XVULNCARD000002 /tokenize HTTP/1.1 Host: TARGET XVULNCARD000003 /tokenize HTTP/1.1 Host: TARGET GET /metrics HTTP/1.1 Host: TARGET HTTP/1.1 200 OK ... http_requests_total{method="XVULNCARD000001",status="4xx",handler="/tokenize"} 1 http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.1",method="XVULNCARD000001",handler="/tokenize"} 1 http_request_duration_seconds_count{method="XVULNCARD000001",handler="/tokenize"} 1 http_request_duration_seconds_sum{method="XVULNCARD000001",handler="/tokenize"} ... ``` Automated: `python poc.py -u http://TARGET:PORT -n 500` sends 500 unique-method requests to `/tokenize` and then scrapes `/metrics`, counting the injected `method="XVULNCARD…"` series before and after. Each unique token contributes several series (counter plus histogram bucket/count/sum lines); the count never decreases afterwards. ### Impact Remote, unauthenticated, cumulative denial of service against deployments that enable the Rust frontend: unbounded and permanent growth of process memory (OOM) plus linearly growing `/metrics` scrape payloads that also stress the Prometheus monitoring stack. Setting `--api-key` does not mitigate the attack because `/tokenize`/`/detokenize` are outside the guarded prefixes. No data confidentiality or integrity impact. vLLM's security policy classifies availability-only issues of this kind as MODERATE.

summary: Denial of service: a negative token id in `/v1/embeddings` or `/pooling` input kills the vLLM engine via a CUDA device-side assertion
description:
### Summary

A single request carrying a **negative token id** in the token-id form of the `input` field of `/v1/embeddings` or `/pooling` terminates the vLLM engine. The request is answered HTTP 500 and the server then serves nothing further: `/health` refuses the connection and every subsequent request from every client fails until the process is restarted.

No authentication, no prior request, and no unusual value are required. `-1` is enough.


### Details

`/v1/embeddings` and `/pooling` accept token ids directly from the caller (`input: list[int] | list[list[int]] | str | list[str]` on `CompletionRequestMixin`, in `vllm/entrypoints/pooling/base/protocol.py`). The engine validated only the **upper** bound of those ids against the vocabulary, in `InputProcessor._validate_model_input`:

```python
if max_input_id > max(tokenizer.max_token_id, model_vocab_size - 1):
    raise ...   # "Token id ... is out of vocabulary"  -> HTTP 400
```

There was no corresponding lower-bound check, so a negative id passed validation and was used directly as an index into the embedding table on the GPU. That trips a device-side assertion inside PyTorch's index kernel:

```
aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/Indexing.cu:1553: indexSelectSmallIndex:
    block: [4,0,0], thread: [32,0,0]
    Assertion `srcIndex < srcSelectDimSize` failed.
```

This is **not** a catchable Python `IndexError`. A CUDA device-side assertion poisons the CUDA context: after it fires, every subsequent CUDA operation in the process fails, including operations belonging to unrelated requests. That is why the process cannot recover and why `/health` refuses the connection rather than answering 503. A `try/except` around the forward pass cannot turn this into a 4xx — the ids have to be bounded **before** they reach the device.

This is not a PyTorch defect. The assertion is PyTorch's protection working as designed; without it an out-of-range id would read unmapped memory. PyTorch checks index *values* host-side only on CPU, because doing so on CUDA would require a synchronization on every indexing op (pytorch/pytorch#71572). The resulting contract is that callers must validate indices before handing them over, and vLLM was not doing so on this path.

### Proof of concept

Against a freshly started server (the first request is a control showing that the token-id input form is legal for this endpoint):

```bash
M=Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B
vllm serve $M --port 8000 --max-model-len 2048 --enforce-eager &

# 1. control -- valid token ids
curl -sS -X POST http://localhost:8000/v1/embeddings \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"model\":\"$M\",\"input\":[[9707,1879]]}"
# -> 200, /health -> 200

# 2. the same request with one id made negative
curl -sS -X POST http://localhost:8000/v1/embeddings \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"model\":\"$M\",\"input\":[[-1,1879]]}"
# -> 500 {"error":{"message":"EngineCore encountered an issue. See stack trace
#          (above) for the root cause.","type":"InternalServerError","code":500}}
# then /health refuses the connection and the server is gone
```

`/pooling` behaves identically. Either list position triggers it, and `-1` behaves the same as `INT64_MIN`, so this is any negative id rather than a boundary value.

### Impact

Any deployment that serves a pooling or embedding model through the OpenAI-compatible API server. One unauthenticated HTTP request is a complete denial of service for that server process and every client using it. Restarting under a supervisor does not mitigate it, because the same request can be sent again immediately.

Confidentiality and integrity are unaffected; the impact is availability only.

### Verification

Measured on stock upstream release images (`vllm/vllm-openai`, aarch64), one request per freshly started server, with a valid control request immediately before the negative one:

| build | endpoint | control | negative id `-1` | `/health` after | valid request after | device-side asserts in log |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **v0.27.1** (unpatched) | `/v1/embeddings` | 200 | **500** | **connection refused** | **connection refused** | 3 |
| **v0.27.1** (unpatched) | `/pooling` | 200 | **500** | **connection refused** | **connection refused** | 3 |
| **v0.28.0** (patched) | `/v1/embeddings` | 200 | **400** `Token id -1 is out of vocabulary` | 200 | 200 | 0 |
| **v0.28.0** (patched) | `/pooling` | 200 | **400** `Token id -1 is out of vocabulary` | 200 | 200 | 0 |

`INT64_MIN` (`-9223372036854775808`) behaves identically to `-1` on both builds, and either position in the id list triggers it, so this is any negative id rather than a boundary value.

On v0.27.1 the engine process reports:

```
torch.AcceleratorError: CUDA error: device-side assert triggered
```

with the underlying kernel assertion being

```
aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/Indexing.cu:1553: indexSelectSmallIndex:
    Assertion `srcIndex < srcSelectDimSize` failed.
```

### Patches

Fixed in **0.28.0** by https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51795 (commit `b216db3ed0`), which adds the missing lower-bound check to `InputProcessor._validate_model_input` so a negative id is rejected as HTTP 400 before the ids reach the device:

```python
if min_input_id < 0:
    raise VLLMValidationError(f"Token id {min_input_id} is out of vocabulary")
```

The validation path is shared by generate, embedding and pooling requests, so the check covers all three.

### Workarounds

For deployments that cannot upgrade to 0.28.0:

- Reject request bodies containing negative integers in `input` at a reverse proxy or API gateway in front of vLLM.
- Do not expose the token-id form of the input; accept only string input from untrusted callers.
- Restrict network access to `/v1/embeddings` and `/pooling`.

Process supervision is **not** a workaround: the request can simply be repeated.

### Not affected

- `/v1/completions` — its `prompt` field constrains token ids with `Field(ge=0)`, so pydantic rejects a negative id before the engine sees it. That constraint has been present since v0.17.0, and was confirmed on an unpatched v0.27.1 build: `CompletionRequest(model=..., prompt=[[-1, 5]])` raises `ValidationError`.
- `/score` and `/rerank` — these do not accept a token-id input form at all.

### References

- https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51795
- https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/71572

summary: GLMGA video sampling permits request-driven CPU and memory exhaustion
description:
## Summary

The OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint accepts request-level video loader options through `media_io_kwargs`. A caller can select the GLMGA sampler and provide large `fps` and `max_frames` values. GLMGA first constructs an attacker-sized Python index list and then deduplicates it, even when the supplied video contains only a few frames. This work occurs in the shared media-loading executor before frame reads, allowing a tiny valid video and compact JSON options to consume disproportionate CPU time and memory and delay unrelated media requests.

The demonstrated impact is partial denial of service. No memory corruption, data disclosure, or code execution is claimed.

## Affected configuration

The server must expose chat completions for a video-capable model and accept request-level `media_io_kwargs`. The model does not need to use GLMGA by default because the request value overrides the model's loader mapping. The proof of concept uses an inline two-frame video and explicitly selects the OpenCV decoder, so no external media host or GPU decoder is required.

The request is reachable without vLLM credentials when no API key is configured. With API-key authentication enabled, any caller holding a valid key can reach the same path.

## Attack surface

A remote caller submits a valid chat-completion request with a small video and the following request-level options:

```json
{
  "media_io_kwargs": {
    "video": {
      "video_backend": "glmga",
      "backend": "opencv",
      "fps": 500000,
      "max_frames": 500000
    }
  }
}
```

Increasing both numeric values increases temporary list construction and deduplication work even when the final decoded frame set remains unchanged.

## Root cause

1. `ChatCompletionRequest` exposes `media_io_kwargs` as request-controlled nested values: [`protocol.py#L365-L371`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/570735520942b6428ae98f1eb442c6d88adae55e/vllm/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/protocol.py#L365-L371).
2. The request options are carried into chat parameters without a numeric work bound on GLMGA's `fps` or `max_frames`: [`protocol.py#L571-L599`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/570735520942b6428ae98f1eb442c6d88adae55e/vllm/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/protocol.py#L571-L599).
3. Media options are merged so request values override configured defaults, including `video_backend`: [`connector.py#L577-L605`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/570735520942b6428ae98f1eb442c6d88adae55e/vllm/multimodal/media/connector.py#L577-L605).
4. The connector selects a registered video loader and runs media loading through the shared executor: [`video.py#L28-L66`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/570735520942b6428ae98f1eb442c6d88adae55e/vllm/multimodal/media/video.py#L28-L66) and [`connector.py#L44-L47`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/570735520942b6428ae98f1eb442c6d88adae55e/vllm/multimodal/media/connector.py#L44-L47).
5. GLMGA calculates `extract_t = min(int(duration * fps), max_frames)`, builds a list with that many entries, and deduplicates it before decoding frames: [`video.py#L667-L740`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/570735520942b6428ae98f1eb442c6d88adae55e/vllm/multimodal/video.py#L667-L740).
6. The OpenCV decoder receives the already-deduplicated indices, so a two-frame file can trigger a large intermediate allocation while producing only two decoded frames: [`opencv.py#L28-L50`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/570735520942b6428ae98f1eb442c6d88adae55e/vllm/multimodal/video_decoders/opencv.py#L28-L50).

The missing invariant is a strict upper bound on sampling work before the index list is constructed. Bounding decoded output after deduplication does not bound the vulnerable intermediate computation.


## Suggested remediation

Validate request-level video sampling options before dispatching work to the media executor. Enforce conservative absolute limits for `fps`, `max_frames`, and especially the computed candidate count. Reject non-finite, negative, or otherwise invalid numeric values.

Avoid constructing `O(extract_t)` intermediate Python lists. Generate bounded unique frame indices directly from the source frame count and output-frame limit. Apply the limit before list construction and before shared executor submission. Add tests showing that extreme request values are rejected or consume constant memory for a fixed output-frame count.

## Workarounds

- Remove or filter request-level `video_backend`, `fps`, and `max_frames` options at the gateway.
- Do not allow untrusted callers to select GLMGA.
- Apply authentication, rate limiting, request concurrency limits, and process memory isolation.
- Use a separate constrained media-loading worker pool where operationally feasible.
- Existing media byte, pixel, or decoded-frame limits do not necessarily bound this pre-decode candidate-index allocation.

## Related advisory

[GHSA-cqm8-jxg6-fqfq](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/security/advisories/GHSA-cqm8-jxg6-fqfq) concerns partial denial of service in the DeepStream video backend through backend confusion and insufficient pixel guarding. This report concerns a different CPU-side GLMGA algorithm: request-controlled sampling values create a large redundant index list before the OpenCV decoder reads a fixed, tiny frame set. The vulnerable backend, resource sink, and required remediation differ.

summary: Request-controlled mm_processor_kwargs.code_revision allows remote code execution
description:
## Summary

An untrusted multimodal request can set `mm_processor_kwargs.code_revision`. When vLLM serves a model whose Hugging Face processor uses dynamic `auto_map` code and the operator enabled `--trust-remote-code`, this request value reaches `AutoProcessor.from_pretrained` and selects the Python revision imported by Transformers.

This lets a client replace the operator-reviewed processor module with code from another revision of the same model repository. The operator-selected model/data `revision` remains pinned; only the executed processor code changes.

Importing a Python module is arbitrary code execution in the vLLM API/renderer process. The PoC below demonstrates this with an import-time filesystem write. It is fully offline and does not require a GPU, model weights, or changes to a real Hub repository.

## Affected snapshot

- Repository: [`vllm-project/vllm`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm)
- Verified commit: [`570735520942b6428ae98f1eb442c6d88adae55e`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/commit/570735520942b6428ae98f1eb442c6d88adae55e)
- Verified with Transformers 5.15.0 and 5.16.1
- Affected release range has not been bisected

## Affected configuration

The vulnerable path exists when all of the following are true:

1. The served model's processor uses dynamic `auto_map.AutoProcessor` code.
2. The operator enabled `trust_remote_code`.
3. The server can fetch the request-selected revision, or it is already cached.
4. The attacker can create or otherwise control a revision in the served model repository. An example is a [Hugging Face community pull-request ref](https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/en/repositories-pull-requests-discussions#where-in-the-git-repo-are-changes-stored) when that repository permits them.
5. A multimodal request reaches the processor path.

The default `trust_remote_code=False` configuration is not affected.

## Attack surface

`mm_processor_kwargs` is accepted directly by public request models:

- [`TokenizeChatRequest.mm_processor_kwargs`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/570735520942b6428ae98f1eb442c6d88adae55e/vllm/entrypoints/serve/tokenize/protocol.py#L111-L114)
- [`ChatCompletionRequest.mm_processor_kwargs`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/570735520942b6428ae98f1eb442c6d88adae55e/vllm/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/protocol.py#L372-L375)

`/tokenize` is particularly relevant because vLLM's authentication middleware guards only `/v1`, `/v2`, `/inference`, and `/cohere` prefixes:

- [`AuthenticationMiddleware`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/570735520942b6428ae98f1eb442c6d88adae55e/vllm/entrypoints/serve/middleware/authenticate.py#L11-L62)

Consequently, `/tokenize` remains unauthenticated even when `--api-key` is configured, unless an external proxy protects it. The vLLM [Security Guide](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/usage/security/#unprotected-endpoints-no-api-key-required) documents `/tokenize` as an unprotected endpoint.

## Root cause

The request value follows this path:

1. [`OnlineRenderer.preprocess_chat`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/570735520942b6428ae98f1eb442c6d88adae55e/vllm/renderers/online_renderer.py#L406-L435) places request `mm_processor_kwargs` in prompt extras.
2. Multimodal rendering forwards those kwargs into processor construction through [`MMProcessorInputs`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/570735520942b6428ae98f1eb442c6d88adae55e/vllm/renderers/base.py#L751-L760) and [`_process_multimodal_async`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/570735520942b6428ae98f1eb442c6d88adae55e/vllm/renderers/base.py#L831-L847).
3. [`MultiModalConfig.merge_mm_processor_kwargs`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/570735520942b6428ae98f1eb442c6d88adae55e/vllm/config/multimodal.py#L506-L518) overlays inference values on startup values, so the request wins.
4. [`cached_get_processor_without_dynamic_kwargs`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/570735520942b6428ae98f1eb442c6d88adae55e/vllm/transformers_utils/processor.py#L344-L375) filters only recognized processor-call keys. `code_revision` is retained as a processor-construction kwarg.
5. [`cached_processor_from_config`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/570735520942b6428ae98f1eb442c6d88adae55e/vllm/transformers_utils/processor.py#L380-L390) pins `revision` and `trust_remote_code`, but forwards the remaining kwargs without reserving `code_revision`.
6. [`get_processor`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/570735520942b6428ae98f1eb442c6d88adae55e/vllm/transformers_utils/processor.py#L205-L245) calls `AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(..., revision=revision, trust_remote_code=trust_remote_code, **kwargs)`.
7. Transformers [`AutoProcessor.from_pretrained`](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/v5.15.0/src/transformers/models/auto/processing_auto.py#L294-L302) uses `code_revision` to retrieve and import the dynamic module through [`get_class_from_dynamic_module`](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/v5.15.0/src/transformers/dynamic_module_utils.py#L474-L575), then removes it before loading processor data. This is why code comes from the attacker revision while configuration/data remain operator-pinned.

Request-time processor arguments are not separated from processor-construction arguments, and `code_revision` is not reserved.

## Security impact

- Confidentiality: High
- Integrity: High
- Availability: High
- Execution context: vLLM API/renderer process

Suggested CVSS v3.1: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H` = **9.8 Critical**

This Base score assumes the affected configuration described above. The [CVSS v3.1 specification](https://www.first.org/cvss/v3.1/specification-document#2-Base-Metrics) scores a vulnerability in that configuration; deployment-specific authentication or network controls belong in Environmental scoring. In an affected deployment, an unauthenticated network client can select and execute arbitrary processor Python inside the vLLM API/renderer process, compromising confidentiality, integrity, and availability. 

## Suggested remediation

1. Separate processor-construction arguments from untrusted processor-call arguments. An allowlist of supported request-time preprocessing controls is safest.
2. Reject `code_revision` and other loader/source controls in request `mm_processor_kwargs`, and pass `model_config.code_revision` explicitly as the only permitted processor-code revision.
3. Add a regression test proving a request cannot change the loaded module revision while operator pins remain effective.
4. Protect `/tokenize` with the configured authentication policy as defense in depth.

Expected safe behavior is either a 4xx response for reserved request keys or silently ignoring them before processor construction. Rejection is preferable because it makes attempted misuse visible.

A patch for this was merged here: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58830

summary: vLLM DoS via unbounded `cache_salt` length: multi-hundred-MB salt stalls the single EngineCore scheduler thread (CPU exhaustion)
description:
### Summary

An unauthenticated remote attacker can exhaust the CPU of the single EngineCore scheduler thread and stall every request on the server by sending HTTP requests with an oversized `cache_salt` parameter. The `cache_salt` field — accepted on the OpenAI-compatible chat completions, completions, responses and pooling endpoints and on the Anthropic `/v1/messages` endpoint — is validated only with `min_length=1` and has **no maximum length**. The full salt string is embedded verbatim into block-0's prefix-cache extra keys and hashed with `sha256(pickle.dumps(...))` **on vLLM's single EngineCore scheduler thread** during request construction, so each request costs O(salt bytes) of serialization plus SHA-256. Measured end-to-end on a live server, a 10 MB salt adds ~58 ms of request latency, 100 MB ~599 ms, and 200 MB ~1195 ms (baseline ~9 ms); under 6 concurrent 100 MB-salt attackers, unrelated ordinary requests are stalled to p90 ≈ 1.8 s / max ≈ 2.5 s (idle median 8.5 ms). Since no HTTP request-body limit is applied by default, a modest stream of such requests keeps the shared scheduler thread busy and denies service to every concurrent tenant. No authentication, no feature flag, and no control-plane/network access are required.

### Details

**Attacker-controlled input reaches the engine hot path with no size bound.**

`cache_salt` is a plain `str` field on four+ API surfaces (latest `main` @ `06569a869`):

```python
# vllm/entrypoints/openai/completion/protocol.py:199-210 (same shape at
#  chat_completion/protocol.py:467, responses/protocol.py:252, anthropic/protocol.py:141)
cache_salt: str | None = Field(
    default=None,
    min_length=1,               # no max_length
    description=(
        "If specified, the prefix cache will be salted with the provided "
        "string to prevent an attacker to guess prompts in multi-user "
        "environments. The salt should be random, protected from "
        "access by 3rd parties, and long enough to be "
        "unpredictable (e.g., 43 characters base64-encoded, corresponding "
        "to 256 bit)."
    ),
)
```

The value flows to `Request` construction in the EngineCore process, where `update_block_hashes()` → `request_block_hasher` (`vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_utils.py:714-771`) computes the request's block hashes — **on the scheduler thread** (`Request.from_engine_core_request`, `vllm/v1/engine/core.py`). For block 0 the entire salt string is placed into the extra keys:

```python
# vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_utils.py:603-606 (generate_block_hash_extra_keys)
cache_salt_keys: list[str] = (
    [request.cache_salt] if (start_token_idx == 0 and request.cache_salt) else []
)
```

and hashed:

```python
# vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_utils.py:620-648 (hash_block_tokens)
return BlockHash(
    hash_function((parent_block_hash, curr_block_token_ids_tuple, extra_keys))
)
# vllm/utils/hashing.py:26-39 (default caching hash function)
input_bytes = pickle.dumps(input, protocol=pickle.HIGHEST_PROTOCOL)
return hashlib.sha256(input_bytes).digest()
```

The salt appears only in block-0's key (so the cost is once per request, not per block), but it is **O(salt bytes)** of pickle serialization plus SHA-256 on the single scheduler thread. Prefix caching (and therefore block hashing) is enabled by default (`enable_prefix_caching=True`), so no non-default flag is needed to reach the sink.

**End-to-end verification (2026-08-29, real server, vllm==0.28.0 default config, RTX PRO 6000):** end-to-end request latency on a live server grows linearly with salt size, and concurrent large-salt requests stall unrelated ordinary requests:

```
baseline (no salt):                  med ≈ 9 ms
cache_salt =  10 MB:                 med ≈ 58 ms
cache_salt =  50 MB:                 med ≈ 301 ms
cache_salt = 100 MB:                 med ≈ 599 ms
cache_salt = 200 MB:                 med ≈ 1195 ms
idle victim (no salt) latency:       med ≈ 8.5 ms
under 3 concurrent 100 MB-salt
attackers, victim (no salt, 10 reqs): med ≈ 22 ms, max ≈ 1465 ms
under 6 concurrent 100 MB-salt
attackers, victim (no salt, 20 reqs): p50 ≈ 33 ms, p90 ≈ 1784 ms, max ≈ 2471 ms
```

No HTTP request-body limit is applied by vLLM by default, so a single replayable request can carry a multi-hundred-MB body. A stream of such requests occupies the scheduler thread; while it is occupied, other requests on the server are not scheduled (queueing, TTFB blowup, client timeouts) — including unrelated tenants that never send a salt.


### Impact

- **Vulnerability type:** unauthenticated remote CPU-exhaustion DoS via an unbounded per-request user field fed into a hot serialization/hash path on the engine's single scheduler thread (CWE-400 / CWE-770 / CWE-20).
- **Impact:** full-service unavailability (scheduling stall) for the duration of the attack; requires no login, no feature flag, no control-plane/network access, and no multi-tenant precondition beyond API reachability.
- **This is the same class as the `n` parameter exhaustion** that vLLM explicitly mitigates: the security guide (`docs/usage/security.md`, "Request Parameter Resource Limits") states "A very large value [of n] causes the engine to allocate memory, CPU, and GPU time proportional to n … To mitigate this, vLLM enforces a configurable upper bound on the n parameter via the VLLM_MAX_N_SEQUENCES environment variable" — and vLLM has published a related advisory for unbounded `n` (GHSA-3mwp-wvh9-7528). `cache_salt` is an equivalent per-request resource-multiplier input with **no bound**; the documented expected value is ~43 chars (256-bit), making a multi-MB salt unambiguously invalid input that should be rejected by validation alone.
- **Who is impacted:** any multi-user deployment that serves the OpenAI-compatible/Anthropic HTTP API — i.e., the standard deployment. The attacker needs only an HTTP client.
